description_full: The Procter & Gamble Company provides branded consumer packaged goods worldwide. It operates through five segments: Beauty; Grooming; Health Care; Fabric & Home Care; and Baby, Feminine & Family Care. The company offers conditioners, shampoos, styling aids, and treatments under the Head & Shoulders, Herbal Essences, Pantene, and Rejoice brands; antiperspirants, deodorants, and personal cleansing products under the Native, Old Spice, Safeguard, and Secret brands; and facial moisturizers, cleaners, and treatments under the Olay and SK-II brands. It also provides blades, razors, shave products, appliances, and other grooming products under the Braun, Gillette, and Venus brands. In addition, the company offers toothbrushes, toothpastes, and other oral care products under the Crest and Oral-B brands; and gastrointestinal, pain relief, rapid diagnostics, respiratory, vitamins/minerals/supplements, and other personal health care products under the Metamucil, Neurobion, Pepto-Bismol, and Vicks brands. Further, it provides fabric enhancers, and laundry additives and detergents under the Ariel, Downy, Gain, and Tide brands; and air and dish care, P&G professional, and surface care under the Cascade, Dawn, Fairy, Febreze, Mr. Clean, and Swiffer brands. Additionally, the company offers baby wipes, taped diapers, and pants under the Luvs and Pampers brands; adult incontinence and menstrual care products under the Always, Always Discreet, and Tampax brands; and paper towels, tissues, and toilet papers under the Bounty, Charmin, and Puffs brands. It sells its products through mass merchandisers, social ecommerce channels, grocery and specialty beauty stores, membership club stores, drug and department stores, distributors, wholesalers, airport duty-free and high-frequency stores, pharmacies, electronics stores, and professional channels, as well as directly to consumers. The company was founded in 1837 and is headquartered in Cincinnati, Ohio.

financial_summary: Procter & Gamble Company (The) is a mega-cap consumer defensive business with a $393.6B market cap on $87.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 7% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $15.1B in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.22× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 23× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 46% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 3 other valuation measures)
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $25.1M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Slow-motion taste and channel shifts — private label, Gen-Z health preferences, or a DTC disruption can erode decade-old brand moats without a single dramatic quarter.
Input cost inflation from agricultural commodities — when raw materials spike, pass-through pricing lags and margin compression is immediate.
GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 6% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 1% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 21% and a beta of 0.44, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.3B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 23% in the 2020 crash, 24% in the 2022 bear market and 39% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $116 (margin of safety -46%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 14%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $91.34 to $152 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 25.6 vs 18.3, EV/EBITDA 16.5 vs 10.2 and P/FCF 26.0 vs 16.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 12% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $174 on average, 2% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 6.9% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.29).
It converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.22x.
ROE of 30% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.4% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($15.4B of cash against $34.1B of debt), with interest covered 22.5x.
The current ratio of 0.68 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
It runs on negative working capital (-43 days), so customers and suppliers effectively fund its operations.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.0% over 3 years, 2.7% over 5 years and 2.9% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 43%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -0.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 5.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 2.7% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 72%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $25.1M sold).
It returns 3.9% a year to shareholders (1.3% in buybacks and 2.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 64 consecutive years, raising it 4.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 104,000 employees, each generates about $837K of revenue, 1.7x the Consumer Defensive median.
That works out to $146K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.4M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
